summary: Defines the Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP), a way of delegating authorization to software and conveying the results and artifacts of that delegation, including access to APIs and subject information.

eli5.summary: It is like giving a valet a key that opens only the car door, and the protocol is how you set what the key can do.

questions: what are bound access tokens in gnap
subtitle: A newer, key-bound way for software to ask for permission, negotiated step by step with an authorization server.

tldr.problem: Software often needs permission to call an API or learn who a user is, but OAuth 2.0 assumes a browser, a fixed grant type per use case and a pre-registered client ID.
tldr.mechanism: The client instance sends one signed JSON request to a single grant endpoint at the authorization server. The two sides then negotiate interaction, consent and continuation over a grant request that moves through defined states, and issued access tokens are bound to the client's key by default.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9635 is a Proposed Standard. It is not an extension of OAuth 2.0 and is not directly compatible with it, so GNAP and OAuth 2.0 will likely exist side by side in many deployments.

today: RFC 9635 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says GNAP is not directly compatible with OAuth 2.0 and that the two will likely exist in parallel in many deployments.

sections.title: What GNAP Is and Who Takes Part
sections.content:
The Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP) lets a piece of software, the client instance, ask for delegated authorization. It can ask for access to APIs on behalf of a resource owner, for subject information about a user, or both. An authorization server (AS) grants the request, usually on behalf of the resource owner. The process is called a grant, and GNAP allows it to be negotiated over time by several parties.

The RFC defines five roles. The AS issues access tokens and other information. The client consumes resources. The resource server (RS) hosts the protected API and accepts only valid access tokens from a trusted AS. The resource owner (RO) may grant or deny operations on resources it has authority over. The end user is the natural person operating the client instance, who may or may not be the RO. One party can fill several roles, and a role can be split across several components.

The RFC separates a client instance, identified by its unique key, from the client software it runs. Many instances of the same software can exist, each with a different key. A cluster that shares one key counts as a single instance.

The focus is interoperability between the parties, not implementation detail. This document covers the client-facing side. How the AS and RS talk to each other is left to a companion document.
sections.eli5: Imagine a coat check. You (the owner) let a helper (the app) pick up your coat, and the person at the desk (the server) decides what the helper may take.

sections.title: The Life of a Grant Request
sections.content:
GNAP is a stateful protocol. The AS owns the state of each grant request, and the RFC names four states: processing, pending, approved and finalized.

  • Processing: entered when a request arrives, when the client updates it, and when interaction completes. The AS decides whether it needs the end user or RO. It must leave this state before it can reply to the client.
  • Pending: approval or interaction is still needed. No access tokens or subject information can be released. The client can poll, or continue after an interaction finishes.
  • Approved: access tokens and subject information can be issued. The client may still send an update, which sends the request back to processing.
  • Finalized: the request is dead and cannot be revived. This happens after a revoke, a denial, a timeout, or when no further updates are allowed. A client that still wants access must start a new grant request.

Because the protocol is stateful, an AS must track the grant request securely itself and must not rely on the client software to track it.
sections.eli5: A grant request is like a pizza order. It is being prepared, waiting on something, ready to eat, or closed. Once it is closed you have to place a brand new order.

sections.title: The Grant Request
sections.content:
To start, the client instance sends an HTTP POST with a JSON document to the AS's grant endpoint. That URI identifies the AS. The request must use Content-Type: application/json unless a key proofing method defines another content type formed from the same JSON. The object has up to five fields:

  • access_token: the rights wanted, as one token object or an array of them. Each token can carry a label and flags. When several tokens are requested, every label must be unique.
  • subject: what to learn about the RO. It lists Subject Identifier formats (sub_id_formats), assertion formats (assertion_formats) such as id_token or saml2, and optionally sub_ids.
  • client: required. It identifies the client instance by value (a key, an optional class_id and display data) or by a reference string.
  • user: optional hints about the end user, by value or reference. These are hints only and must not be taken as proof that a particular RO is present.
  • interact: the ways the client can start interaction, finish it and hint at locales.

Tokens are key-bound by default. The client asks for a bearer flag only if it wants an unbound token. The access array describes rights as objects with a required type and optional common fields actions, locations, datatypes, identifier and privileges, or as plain strings. The RFC says its structure is analogous to the Rich Authorization Requests of RFC 9396, and that strings play a role like OAuth scopes.

The AS treats unknown client keys in its own way: it may allow the request and require the RO to authorize it (trust on first use), limit what is offered, or reject it with invalid_client. A client must never send a symmetric key by value. The display and class_id values are self-declared and are only hints.
sections.eli5: The app fills in one form saying what it wants, who it is, and how you can be reached, and it signs the form so the server knows it is the same app next time.

sections.title: The Grant Response
sections.content:
The AS replies with a JSON object and the header Cache-Control: no-store. Its possible fields are continue, access_token, interact, subject, instance_id and error.

Continuation. The continue object holds a URI, an optional wait in seconds, and a continuation access token. That token must be bound to the client's key and must not be a bearer token. If wait is omitted, the client must treat it as five seconds, and the value should not be below five.

Access tokens. Each token has an opaque value, the granted access, and optionally a label, an expires_in lifetime, a key, flags and a manage object for token management. The flags defined here are bearer and durable. A durable token is a hint that a previous token keeps working after rotation or a grant modification. A client must reject a token that has the bearer flag and also a key. The granted rights may differ from what was requested.

Subject information. The AS returns sub_ids and/or assertions only when it is sure the RO and the end user are the same party. A returned email or phone identifier names the RO to the AS. It must not be used as a way to contact the person. A client must read subject information in the context of the AS that issued it, because two servers can use the same identifier for different people.

Instance identifier. The AS may return an instance_id so the client can later send that string instead of the full client object. It must be kept secret.
sections.eli5: The server's answer is like a ticket stub: it can hold a key to a locker, a note saying wait here, or a polite no with a reason.

sections.title: Interaction and Consent
sections.content:
How the AS decides is out of scope, but GNAP defines common patterns. The AS can approve straight away, deny, or move the request to pending and gather consent. It can start interaction through the client, challenge the client, contact the RO out of band (a push notification, for instance), or apply an RO's automated policy. It may even require more than one RO to approve.

The client lists the ways it can start interaction under interact.start, and the AS replies with data for the modes it supports. Each mode may be used at most once.

  • redirect: the AS returns a unique URI. The client must not change it or add parameters.
  • app: the AS returns a URI for an application on the user's device.
  • user_code: a short code typed at a stable URI, usually on a second device. Codes are case-insensitive, randomly generated, short lived, and recommended to be six to eight characters.
  • user_code_uri: a short code plus a short dynamic URI.

To learn when the RO is done, the client can ask for a finish method. With redirect the browser returns to the client's callback URI by GET. With push the AS sends an HTTP POST. Either way the callback carries an interact_ref and a hash.

The interaction hash ties the callback to the right request. It is built from four lines joined by a newline: the client's nonce, the AS's nonce, the interact_ref and the grant endpoint URI. This is hashed with sha-256 unless hash_method says otherwise, then encoded as base64url without padding. The client must validate it and must not send the interact_ref on if validation fails. Because the grant endpoint is in the hash, it also guards against an attacker swapping in a different AS.
sections.eli5: The app hands you a claim ticket with a secret number on it. When you come back from the front desk, the desk stamps the ticket, and the app checks the stamp before it believes you.

sections.title: Continuing, Modifying and Discovering
sections.content:
A grant request often needs several round trips. The AS provides a continuation API at the URI in continue. Every call presents the continuation access token in an Authorization: GNAP header and is signed with the client's key. Continuation tokens cannot be used at an RS, and other tokens cannot be used for continuation.

  • Continue after interaction: a POST with the one-time interact_ref. A client that sends it when the request is not pending gets too_many_attempts, and the AS should finalize the request.
  • Polling: a POST with no content, honoring wait. A client that polls too early gets too_fast.
  • Modify: an HTTP PATCH with new access_token, subject, interact or user fields. The AS moves the request back to processing. Earlier tokens are not changed. Anything issued is a new, independent token.
  • Revoke: an HTTP DELETE, answered with 204. The request becomes finalized and the AS should revoke related tokens.

Each continuation response should carry a new continuation token that replaces the old one. If no continue field comes back, the client must not make another continuation request.

Discovery is deliberately light. A client only needs the grant endpoint and its keys. It can send an HTTP OPTIONS request to the grant endpoint to learn supported features, but that information is only an optimization and the AS may still deny a request. In the RS-first method, an RS answers a request that lacks a valid token with a WWW-Authenticate GNAP challenge containing as_uri, referrer and access. The RFC warns that a compromised RS could misuse this and suggests pre-registration as an alternative.
sections.eli5: After the first chat, the app keeps a special pass to knock on the server's door again, and each new pass replaces the one before it.

sections.title: Managing Access Tokens
sections.content:
If an access token comes with a manage object, the client may call its management URI. Only two actions are defined, rotate and revoke. The management URI must not contain the token value, and calls are protected by a separate token management access token plus proof of the key.

Rotation. A POST with no content asks for a new token with the same rights and properties but a new value and expiry. The AS must invalidate the old value if it can, and answers 200 with the new token. The rights cannot be changed in a rotation. To get different rights, the client updates the grant request or starts a new one. If the AS cannot rotate, it returns invalid_rotation.

Rotating the key. To bind a new key to a token, the client sends the new key in the body and must prove both keys at once. The old key's signature must cover the new key. The new key's signature must cover the old signature. The proofing method cannot change, and a bearer token has no key to rotate. If the AS does not support this it returns key_rotation_not_supported.

Revocation. An HTTP DELETE to the management URI asks the AS to invalidate the token. A successful call returns 204. The AS should treat the request as valid even if the token has already expired.
sections.eli5: Rotating a token is like swapping your hotel key card for a fresh one that opens the same doors. Revoking is handing the card back so it stops working.

sections.title: Proving Possession of a Key
sections.content:
GNAP secures requests with an access token, a key proof, or both. A token with a proof is a bound token request. A proof alone starts a grant. A token alone is a bearer request, allowed only at an RS and only for unbound tokens. With neither, the request is unsecured, which is used optionally in RS-first discovery.

A key sent by value is always a public key in exactly one format: jwk (which must include alg and kid, with alg never none), cert or cert#S256. A key can also be a reference string that points to key material the AS knows about, and keys referenced this way may be shared symmetric keys. Symmetric keys must not be passwords or derived from one.

Access tokens travel in the Authorization header with the GNAP scheme, together with the proof. A bearer token uses Authorization: Bearer as in RFC 6750, and the form-body and query-string methods of that RFC must not be used.

Four proofing methods are defined. Every method must cover the URI, the HTTP method, relevant headers and the message content, and the verifier must check all of it. When a proof is tied to a token, the token itself must be covered.

With httpsig, the signature follows RFC 9421 and must cover @method and @target-uri. It also covers content-digest (per RFC 9530) when there is a body, and authorization when a token is used. The tag parameter must be gnap, and created must be close to the current time. A nonce should be included.
sections.eli5: Showing a key proof is like signing your name every time you use your pass, so a thief who finds the pass cannot use it without your signature.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats authorization requests as security and privacy sensitive, with long sections on both. Several points stand out.

  • TLS is still needed. Signing does not protect requests from interception. All requests over untrusted networks must use TLS, including calls to an RS that use key-bound tokens.
  • Bearer tokens are discouraged. Any party that captures one can use it, and any RS that receives one can replay it elsewhere. GNAP makes key-bound tokens the default. One pattern the RFC describes is a gateway that checks signatures on the outside and passes bearer tokens only to trusted internal systems.
  • Key-bound tokens help only if the RS checks. The RS must validate the signature, ensure the right key was used for that token and ensure enough of the message is covered.
  • Mix-up attacks. A rogue AS could proxy a client's request to a real AS. The interaction hash includes the grant endpoint to block this, but only if the client validates it. A client that talks to several ASes should use a different key for each.
  • Client-supplied user data is a hint. The AS cannot tell from it that the person is present.

The privacy section is modeled on the threats in RFC 6973 and covers surveillance, stored data, intrusion, correlation and disclosure in shared references.
sections.eli5: A signed pass is safer than a plain one, but you still need a locked tunnel to walk through, or people can watch you and copy things.

sections.title: How GNAP Differs from OAuth 2.0
sections.content:
GNAP solves many of the same use cases as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. It is not an extension of OAuth 2.0 and is not meant to be directly compatible with it, though the RFC gives examples for mapping OAuth scopes and client IDs onto GNAP. Appendix A lists six differences.

  • Consent flexibility: OAuth generally assumes the user has a browser and is the same person who approves. GNAP lets the client list how it can start and finish interaction, and allows the end user and RO to be different people.
  • Inline negotiation: OAuth uses grant types that start at different endpoints. GNAP starts every request at one endpoint and negotiates the next steps.
  • Client instances: OAuth requires a registered client_id. GNAP lets a client present an unknown key.
  • Expanded delegation: GNAP has a rich access structure, with string references as a shortcut, and a way to request subject information apart from API access.
  • Cryptographic security: every client-to-AS call is bound to a key, and GNAP has no notion of public clients.
  • Privacy: GNAP is meant to work with decentralized identity standards and to avoid consolidation around a few popular AS services.

The RFC also notes that refresh tokens are not needed when token rotation is available.
sections.eli5: OAuth is like many different doors for different visitors. GNAP is one front door where you explain who you are and what you need, and the doorman works out the rest.

items.label: Bad request
items.desc: Missing parameter, invalid value or malformed request.

items.label: Unknown client
items.desc: Client not recognized or allowed, or its signature failed.

items.label: Bad interaction
items.desc: Wrong interaction reference, or interaction modes expired.

items.label: Bad flags
items.desc: The flag configuration is not valid.

items.label: Bad rotation
items.desc: The token rotation request is not valid.

items.label: No key rotation
items.desc: The AS does not allow rotating this token's key.

items.label: Bad continuation
items.desc: The continuation of the grant could not be processed.

items.label: RO said no
items.desc: The resource owner denied the request.

items.label: Unknown user
items.desc: User not known, or not the user present in the interaction.

items.label: Unverified interaction
items.desc: The interaction integrity could not be established.

items.label: Polled too early
items.desc: The client ignored the wait period.

items.label: Too many tries
items.desc: A limit on reasonable attempts was reached.

messages.label: Authenticate and authorize

messages.label: Continue request
